facts.text: The authors used spray-drying followed by thermal decomposition-reduction to synthesize noble-metal high-entropy-alloy three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
They varied Pt:Ru ratios from 3:1 to 1:4 and applied secondary heating at 400 or 500°C to tune fcc and hcp phase fractions in PtxNiCoCuRuy nanoframeworks.
The standard reduction treatment heated the spray-dried precursors in H2 at 3°C/min to 300°C, held them for 30 min, and then cooled them at 5–10°C/min.
Methanol oxidation was tested in deoxygenated 0.5 M H2SO4 containing 0.5 M CH3OH by cyclic voltammetry at 50 mV/s.
The synthesis produced porous, self-supported three-dimensional nanoframeworks assembled from nanoarms, with generally homogeneous elemental distributions and single-phase solid-solution lattices.

The proposed formation mechanism was that Pt, Ir, or Ru reduced first, dissociated H2 on the newborn noble-metal surface, and supplied reactive hydrogen atoms that reduced nearby Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe for incorporation into the pre-existing lattice.
Pd did not enable the same single-phase formation because hydrogen desorption from Pd was calculated to be unfavorable and to have a higher barrier.
In Pt–Ru alloys, secondary heating enabled the kinetically retained Pt-based fcc structure to overcome an approximately 0.45-eV barrier and transform toward the more stable Ru-based hcp structure.
The PtNiCoCuRuIr nanoframework showed higher methanol-oxidation mass activity and maintained a higher chronoamperometric current than commercial Pt black throughout the measured interval.
PtNiCoCuRuIr reached 2637 mA/mgPt, approximately 15 times the 170 mA/mgPt mass activity of commercial Pt black.
Increasing Ru content and secondary-heating temperature increased the hcp fraction, and Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru4 became predominantly hcp after reheating at 500°C.
In situ STEM of Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru4 showed hcp structure appearing near 350°C and complete local fcc-to-hcp conversion by 400°C.
